extracted.intended_audience: patent judges, patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and appellate counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and interpretive criteria for construing patent claim terms (Fed. Cir. en banc guidance). Explains the relative weight of intrinsic and extrinsic evidence, how to treat dictionaries, specification, prosecution history, and related doctrines (claim differentiation, preserving validity, importing limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as primary guide
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is 'the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed term' and 'acts as a dictionary when it expressly defines terms used in the claims or when it defines terms by implication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the specification in every case; give it primary weight in determining claim term meaning. Do not treat dictionary definitions as dispositive if they conflict with meanings ascertainable from the patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary meaning in context of entire patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ordinary meaning' of a claim term is its meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art after reading the entire patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim terms based on how a POSITA would understand them in the context of the claims, specification, and prosecution history—not based on an abstract dictionary definition divorced from context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence priority (claims, specification, prosecution history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (the claims, specification, and prosecution history) is the primary source for claim construction and should be the main focus at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by examining how the patentee used the term in the claims, specification, and prosecution history. This approach reduces the risk of adopting an unduly expansive construction derived from extrinsic sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted but subordinate use of dictionaries and treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries, technical treatises, and other extrinsic sources may be consulted to assist understanding, but they must not contradict definitions found in or ascertained from the patent documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic sources can help understand commonly understood meanings or the technology, and are accessible beforehand, but treat their definitions with caution and subordinate to intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of excessive reliance on dictionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy reliance on dictionaries focuses inquiry on abstract meanings rather than on claim meaning within patent context and may transform a claim term's meaning to its abstract dictionary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting with broad dictionary definitions and then narrowing; general dictionaries collect many uses (common to obscure), which can lead to overbroad constructions inconsistent with the patentee's disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical dictionaries and treatises are not definitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even technical dictionaries or treatises may not reflect how the patentee used a term; there is no guarantee a term is used the same way in a treatise as by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technical extrinsic references to understand technology, but do not allow them to override intrinsic evidence; recognize that patent descriptions may use terms in novel ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may define terms implicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification may define claim terms by implication even when guidance is not provided in explicit definitional format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for implicit definitions and usages in the specification; the absence of an explicit 'defined as' phrase does not preclude the specification from defining a term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing limitations from specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must avoid reading limitations from the specification into the claims; there is a fine line between construing a claim in light of the specification and importing limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between exemplary embodiments used to teach/enable and limitations that should be read into the claims. Focus on whether a POSITA would understand the specification to restrict the claim scope to the embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of specification (teach, enable, best mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification's purposes are to teach and enable those of skill in the art to make and use the invention and to provide a best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep these purposes in mind when interpreting whether embodiments are illustrative or limiting; examples often illustrate how to practice the invention rather than define claim boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation (dependent claims inform scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim’s inclusion of a specific limitation makes it likely the independent claim does not contain that limitation (to avoid redundancy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of narrower limitations in dependent claims as evidence that the broader independent claim was intended to be broader; do not read limitations into independent claims that would render dependent claims redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple objectives in specification do not narrowly limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent stating several objectives does not require that each claim be construed as limited to structures capable of achieving all objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification lists multiple purposes or advantages for an element, do not construe the claim to require that the element perform every listed purpose unless the claim language or specification clearly so requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of construing to preserve validity is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be construed to preserve validity only where, after applying all claim construction tools, the claim remains ambiguous and it is reasonable to infer the PTO would not have issued an invalid patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not routinely factor validity into claim construction; only apply this maxim when (1) ambiguity remains after full construction, (2) the proposed construction is practicable and based on sound principles, and (3) it does not revise or ignore explicit claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rigid algorithm or required sequence of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no magic formula or mandated sequence for consulting sources; courts are not barred from considering any particular sources or required to analyze them in any specific sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges may consult dictionaries, extrinsic references, and intrinsic evidence in any order, but must assign appropriate weight to each source in accordance with patent law policies and must not use extrinsic sources to contradict unambiguous intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries cannot overcome art-specific intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A general-usage dictionary cannot overcome art-specific evidence of the meaning of a claim term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intrinsic (art-specific) evidence indicates a particular meaning, that meaning controls over generic dictionary definitions; judges should not let dictionary editor preferences determine claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence useful for understanding technology only
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges may consult extrinsic sources at any time to better understand the underlying technology, but reliance on them for construction must not contradict intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extrinsic materials to illuminate technical background and ordinary skill in the art; do not permit extrinsic evidence to supersede the meaning established by the patent documents.
